description:
We are an Egyptian team that wants to join this competition. We have skills in web development, graphic design, coding, software, hardware, and more.

As students at a STEM school, we are interested in building projects and design. Others should join our team because we have a wide range of skills that can help them improve theirs, too.
summary:
AEGIS is offline health-monitoring software that helps astronauts understand their own health during long missions, when Earth is minutes away and no doctor is on board. It needs no wearables or special hardware. Each day the astronaut types readings from the habitat’s medical kit (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, breathing rate, blood pressure, glucose), answers a short check-in about sleep, mood, stress and symptoms, and uses a webcam for fatigue and blink-rate signals. Cabin data such as CO2 is read alongside.

AEGIS learns a personal “normal” for each astronaut, so it compares every person with themselves, not with one fixed limit for everyone. It gives a clear state: NORMAL, WATCH or ACT. It explains why, gives guidance written from NASA Human Research Program pages, and asks for a re-measure before raising an emergency.

In a 20-mission simulation it found all 26 health declines, with a median of 3 days, and raised zero false ACT alerts. This matters because crews on Moon and Mars missions must find problems early and handle them on their own.
details:
AEGIS runs on any laptop with a keyboard, mouse and webcam, with no internet. It has five steps:

  1. Enter. The astronaut enters readings from the medical kit. Every field shows how to measure it. A daily check-in covers sleep hours, mood, stress words and symptoms. The webcam gives a fatigue score and blink rate. Cabin data (CO2, O2, pressure, radiation) comes from the habitat.
  2. Check the entry. Before anything is judged, AEGIS checks the data itself. It catches missing values, impossible values (for example 3.67 °C instead of 36.7), values copied unchanged for days, and readings saved under the wrong astronaut’s profile. An entry error is never read as illness.
  3. Learn a personal baseline. For the first 14 days, AEGIS learns each astronaut’s normal range. After that it re-learns every week from recent healthy days. A fixed anchor stops it from slowly “getting used to” a real decline.
    • a sudden safety problem;
    • a slow decline (ACT only after it lasts two days);
    • a cabin problem that affects the whole crew.
  4. Guide. The result is NORMAL, WATCH or ACT, with the reason in plain words. It comes with a guidance card (what it means, what to do now, how to improve) written from NASA HRP pages, and gives no medicine doses. There is also a clickable body self-check by symptoms, daily health tasks with points and a streak, and a short ready-to-send message for the flight surgeon on Earth. Everything is available in English and Arabic.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Problems are found earlier: in testing, every health decline was found, a median of 3 days in. Fixed limits found 20 of 26, with a median of 9.5 days.
  • Alarms are trusted: there were 0 false ACT alerts, 0 of 9 single bad nights reached ACT, and 0 of 33 entry errors were read as illness.
  • The crew gets more independence. Astronauts understand their own health and know what to do while waiting for Earth.
  • Flight surgeons get a short, clear summary instead of raw numbers.
  • The same approach can reach Earth: remote stations, polar bases, submarines and rural clinics with no doctor on site.

Tools and languages

  • Engine: Python (standard library), unit-tested with pytest (48 tests).
  • Server: FastAPI and Uvicorn, plus a fully offline server.
  • Webcam signals: OpenCV.
  • Interface: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Code: Git and GitHub.

No hardware sensors are used. All astronaut data in the demo is simulated: a 125-day mission with three astronauts, plus a 20-mission evaluation.

Creativity

  • AEGIS compares each astronaut with himself, not with an average person.
  • It checks the data before it judges the person.
  • It asks for a re-measure before it calls an emergency.
  • It tells a personal problem apart from a cabin problem that affects the whole crew.
  • It turns monitoring into a daily routine the astronaut takes part in: entry, self-check, tasks and a message to Earth.

Factors we considered

  • Astronaut workload: daily entry takes a few minutes.
  • No internet and communication delay.
  • Avoiding false alarms that make the crew ignore alerts.
  • Privacy: data stays on the habitat computer.
  • Safety: it is not a diagnostic tool, gives no medicine doses, and the flight surgeon makes the final decision.
  • Honest limits: the data is simulated and some thresholds need clinical review.
